Charles Cornwallis. The senior British general in the later stages of the American Revolution and the commander of British forces at Yorktown, where his surrender in 1781 effectively ended the war.

Cornwallis took command of the southern theater after the British capture of Charleston and pursued an aggressive strategy of invasion and control, seeking to rally loyalists and defeat the Continental Army in decisive battle. He grew frustrated by Nathanael Greene's strategy of evasion and attrition, winning pitched battles such as Camden in 1780 but losing control of the region as his supply lines were cut and his army weakened.

In 1781, he retreated into Virginia in pursuit of Lafayette's small force, only to find himself trapped by Washington's approach from the north and a French fleet blockading his escape by sea. After a brief siege, he surrendered at Yorktown in October of 1781, effectively ending major combat operations and securing American independence.

Despite his defeat, Cornwallis was respected even by the Americans as an honorable opponent and a capable professional. Rather than blame his soldiers, he attributed the defeat to lack of naval support and strategic overextension.

After the war, he served as Governor-General of India and continued his career with distinction, dying as a respected elder statesman of the British Empire.
